title: Tamlaght O’Crilly: the Hugh households
standfirst: The Pennsylvania emigrant Hugh is now assessed as the probable son of Hugh Glasgow and Margaret McCullough. The two 1740 Hugh household identities remain open. The earlier William–John–Hugh pedigree is assessed as probable within the family account, with its separate identity questions retained.
question: Which, if any, later Glasgow family belongs to each documented Hugh household?
answer: The explicit descendant account and independently matching Pennsylvania household support probable Hugh–McCullough parentage for the younger emigrant Hugh. The 1740 return establishes an older local surname generation, but neither entry is identified conclusively with his father. The older John and William ancestry remains separate and unproved.

chapters.title: 1725 Cavankilgreen: the Glasgows are adjoining occupiers
body: Research rationale: read the original to test whether the abstract omitted William or John’s forename, and separate the actual recorded occupants from a desired pedigree connection.

23 October 2026 original deed review: memorial 71,498, volume 101, p. 337, reads **“the Glasgows”**, collectively, as adjoining occupiers in Cavankilgreen, Tyrone. No personal forename is visible to recover; these occupiers are not the named lessees of the seventeen acres. The Falls lives are not Glasgow children. [Original reading and family boundary](/branches/research-irish-tamlaght/#tyrone-deed-71498). William-591 and John-551 remain compatible family comparisons only; no individual identification or father grade changes.

The original property clause describes land lying between a road (destination uncertain) and another portion possessed by the Glasgows, together with half the Bogg Meadow. The preferred plural reading is a collective surname reference, not a recovered individual name. The leased land contains seventeen Scotch acres, English measure, in the manuscript’s wording; no conversion is inferred. The Falls children named as lives are not Glasgow relatives.

This supersedes the earlier original-unread question. The useful next test is the separate Glasgow holding in Moore estate/deed succession at this locality. Neither the late William pedigree nor the son John is identified merely by this county/surname context.

chapters.period: Earlier traditional generations · two probable fathers
chapters.title: The earlier Tyrone pedigree: probable William–John–Hugh father roles
body: The family history explicitly calls John a son of William and introduces Hugh, the Tyrone-born weaver, among John’s sons. These are specific parent statements in a continuous pedigree, not parents supplied from a shared surname. The nearer part of that account identifies the Hugh–McCullough family and the younger Hugh’s Pennsylvania household, whose children agree with the independently inspected 1827 will. That household correlation supports the account’s family knowledge without independently proving the two earlier fathers. With the retained generations compatible and no conflicting parent account identified for these traditional roles, William–John and John–Hugh warrant probable local assessments. The preference is for the particular family-history accounts, not an identification with other same-name Scottish or Irish records.

Both earlier father names come from one later family narrative; they are not two independent confirmations. John’s circa-1681 birth is calculated and William’s circa-1655/1656 date is estimated, so neither is corroboration. The 1740 return cannot distinguish the two Hugh householders or name their parents. No contemporary record identifies John-551 or William-591 in these roles. The narrative’s Cameron surname-origin and 1689 military story are unverified and are not used as parentage evidence. William’s selected uncertain Inveresk/Cavers identity and Robert-2462 father hypothesis remain separate. John-3960’s very uncertain placement and the alternative that the two Johns are one person remain unchanged. No mother, wife, new date, migration or exact 1740 identity is inferred.

Two existing unmarked/ungraded father links become probable local assessments. No new attachment, documented/certain upgrade, merge or live WikiTree edit is made. Their child sides contain 47 and 43 pre-1850 profiles respectively; these nested impacts overlap and must not be added. All other parent IDs and grades, including the older Scottish and Leitrim hypotheses, are preserved.

chapters.title: Hugh’s probable parents: Hugh Glasgow and Margaret McCullough
body: Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded.

Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

This is a review of two existing parent links, not two new attachments or newly discovered records. Both prior effective flags were unmarked and the local assessments unknown; the new formal local grade is probable, below documented or confidently marked parentage. The father edge supports 40 retained pre-1850 profiles and 39,800 connected pairs across the fixed working tree; that is branch impact, not a probability, and overlapping edge impacts must not be added. All parent IDs, vital fields, working family membership, selected hypotheses and confidently marked connectivity remain unchanged. The scanned family history pp.2–3 and original recorded will pp.492–493 were re-read for this review. The 1740 return uses its maintained earlier reading. No live WikiTree edit or identity merge is made.

chapters.period: 1639–1689 · two very uncertain fathers through possible identity
chapters.title: William Glasgow: a conditional Polwarth–Cavers–Ulster family
body: Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man.

The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

The weakest stage is the proposed father’s identity. Glasgow-2462 was born at Inveresk on 20 August 1639 and baptised the next day. He would have been only 18 at the 1658 Polwarth baptism and 16, nearly 17, at the associated Elizabeth baptism in August 1656. Young fatherhood is possible, but there is no marriage, residence or occupation connecting him with the named Polwarth father. An older, otherwise unidentified William is a substantial competing explanation. The named-child clause does not prove Glasgow-2462’s identity. The regional Polwarth/Gordon household of Glasgow-3107 is a stronger local kinship lead than Inveresk alone, but supplies no father clause for William; no exact brother, uncle or father relationship with James is selected. This inherited father remains a very low-confidence default and would fall away on both new adult accounts if the child/father identification fails. No mother is selected for either adult, and no wife or mother is transferred from the Inveresk ancestry.

This conditional Scottish parent model does not identify either of the two Hugh householders in the 1740 Tamlaght O’Crilly return. The inherited Glasgow-591 → Glasgow-551 → Glasgow-548 family-history sequence remains a separate question. The 1740 return and the 1772 parish declaration provide no evidence for the new Scottish father selections. No Tamlaght household identity or parent relationship becomes certain. See the complete comparison in Early Scottish records.

chapters.title: Two householders, not one family
body: The Protestant-householders return records two separate Hugh Glasgow entries, numbered 1195 and 1272 in the collector-order transcription. Both have townland recorded as ‘Not specified’.
The distinction is evidence against merging the entries. Age, occupation, wife, children and relationship are absent.

evidence.label: 1740 return transcription

chapters.title: A geographic lead, not an address
body: Entry 1272 falls in a collector sequence with names independently found in the Inishrush leasehold community. A 1734 lease identifies several of those people at Inishrush, but no Glasgow is named.
That makes the sequence an Inishrush-linked lead; it does not make Hugh a stated resident or Margaret McCullough’s husband.

evidence.label: 1734 Inishrush lease, memorial 57951

chapters.title: One later parish occurrence
body: A declaration dated at Innisrush names Hugh Glasgow among people described collectively as inhabitants of Tamlaght O’Crilly parish.
The notice gives no Hugh-specific townland, age or relatives. It could concern either older householder, the younger emigrant Hugh, or another namesake.

evidence.label: Belfast News-Letter transcription

chapters.title: A family history stays qualified
body: The later family history now supports probable traditional father roles and the separately assessed Hugh–McCullough parents. It does not select either 1740 householder or make the Scottish and Leitrim identities certain.
The younger Hugh’s 1827 will establishes his later Pennsylvania household, but does not name his parents or an Irish connection to the recorded householders.
